question: What first drew you to theatre, and when did you know you wanted to study it seriously?
lookingFor: A specific, personal moment of discovery rather than a vague love of performing.

bullets: Name a concrete production, class, or experience that sparked it
Explain what specifically about that moment stayed with you
Show the line from that spark to actively pursuing it since
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I was cast as a background villager in a school production of Our Town when I was twelve, and I remember standing in the wings watching the stage manager character talk directly to the audience and feeling the whole room go still. That was the first time I understood theatre could do something a screen couldn't. Since then I've tried to be in or around a production every term, from backstage crew to eventually directing a one-act myself.

commonMistakes: Saying 'I've always loved performing' with no specific moment
Describing only watching TV or film, with no live theatre
Treating the question as a formality rather than reflecting
followUps: Has your reason for loving theatre changed since then?

question: Why do you want to study Drama and Theatre at our institution rather than go straight into a drama school or conservatoire route?
lookingFor: A clear understanding of the difference between an academic theatre degree and vocational training, and why the applicant wants this path.

bullets: Show awareness of what an academic course offers that a conservatoire doesn't
Reference something specific about the course structure or staff
Connect it to the applicant's own goals, not just a fallback choice
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I want the chance to study theatre history and dramaturgy alongside practice, not just train as a performer, because I'm as interested in why a play works as in being in it. Your course's third-year devising module, where students build an original piece from research rather than an existing script, is exactly the kind of combination I'm after. I looked at conservatoire training too, but I want the wider critical grounding first, and this course is structured to give me both.

commonMistakes: Implying the applicant only ended up here because they didn't get into drama school
Not knowing the difference between a BA and conservatoire training
Generic praise that could apply to any theatre course
followUps: What would you do if the course turned out to be more academic than practical?

question: Tell us about the last piece of theatre you saw. What did you think of it?
lookingFor: Genuine, recent engagement with live theatre and the ability to form and articulate a critical opinion, not just a plot summary.

bullets: Name a specific production, venue, and roughly when you saw it
Give an actual opinion, not just a summary of the plot
Justify the opinion with something concrete from staging, performance, or text
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I saw a touring production of A Streetcar Named Desire a few months ago, and what stayed with me was the design choice to keep the apartment set slightly too small for the actors, so everyone was always physically close. I thought it worked brilliantly for the claustrophobia of the play, though I found the pacing dragged in the second act. It made me think a lot about how a director's spatial choices can do as much storytelling as the dialogue.

commonMistakes: Only summarising the plot with no opinion
Naming something seen years ago with no recent theatre-going
Giving an opinion with no reasoning behind it
followUps: What would you have done differently if you were directing it?

question: What roles have you taken on in productions so far, on stage or off?
lookingFor: Genuine, varied hands-on experience and honest reflection on what each role taught the applicant.

bullets: List real, specific roles rather than a vague 'I've done a bit of everything'
Reflect on what each role taught, not just what it was
Show range across performing and non-performing work if possible
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've mostly performed, including playing Lady Macbeth in a school production last year, but I also stage-managed a community theatre run of a new play, which taught me how much of a show depends on decisions nobody in the audience ever notices, like cue timing. Doing both sides has made me a better performer because I now think about the whole picture, not just my own lines. I'd like to try lighting design next, since I've never had a chance to work on that side.

commonMistakes: Only listing performing roles with no other production experience
Vague claims like 'I've done lots of theatre' with no specifics
No reflection on what was learned from each role
followUps: Which of those roles suited you least, and why?

question: Have you read any theatre theory or criticism beyond your set texts? What did you take from it?
lookingFor: Evidence of intellectual curiosity about theatre beyond required coursework, with genuine understanding rather than name-dropping.

bullets: Name a specific writer, theorist, or book, not just a vague genre
Explain the core idea in the applicant's own words
Connect it to how it changed how they watch or make theatre
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I read Peter Brook's The Empty Space after a teacher recommended it, and his idea of 'deadly theatre,' work that goes through the motions without any real engagement, completely changed how I judge productions I see. It made me start noticing when a well-funded show still feels lifeless because nobody on stage seems to actually need to be saying their lines. I've since tried to apply that idea in my own acting, asking myself before every scene why my character needs this moment right now.

commonMistakes: Naming a theorist without being able to explain the idea
Only citing texts that were assigned, calling them wider reading
No connection made between the theory and the applicant's own practice
followUps: Do you disagree with anything in what you read?

question: What do you understand by the Stanislavski system, and where have you tried to apply it?
lookingFor: A working understanding of key concepts like objective, given circumstances, and emotional truth, plus evidence of applying them in practice.

bullets: Explain at least one core concept accurately, such as objectives or given circumstances
Avoid conflating Stanislavski with unrelated later methods
Give a concrete example of using it in rehearsal or performance
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The part I find most useful is objectives, working out what your character actually wants in a scene and letting every line serve that want, rather than just performing emotions in the abstract. When I played a character who was lying to her sister, I built the whole scene around her objective of protecting the sister from a truth, which changed how I delivered lines that had seemed flat before. It stopped me from playing generic sadness and gave me something active to do instead.

commonMistakes: Confusing Stanislavski with Method acting as practiced by later American teachers
Reciting the term with no real understanding of what it means in practice
No example of actually applying it
followUps: How does an objective differ from an emotion?

question: Can you explain what Brecht meant by the alienation effect, and why he wanted it?
lookingFor: Correct understanding that alienation, or Verfremdungseffekt, aims to stop audiences losing themselves emotionally so they think critically instead.

bullets: Define alienation as deliberately breaking emotional immersion
Explain the political purpose behind it, encouraging critical thought over passive absorption
Give a concrete technique used to achieve it, such as direct address or visible stagecraft
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Brecht wanted audiences to watch a play thinking critically about the situation on stage rather than getting swept up emotionally, because he believed emotional absorption made people passive about the social problems being shown. He used techniques like actors stepping out of character to address the audience directly, or keeping the stage lighting rig visible, to keep reminding people they were watching a construction. I find it a really different goal from Stanislavski, who wants the audience to feel everything is real, and I like that theatre can choose either aim depending on what it's trying to say.

commonMistakes: Saying alienation just means making the audience feel uncomfortable or bored
Missing the political motivation behind the technique
Confusing it with breaking the fourth wall as a purely comic device
followUps: Can you think of a modern production that uses a similar technique?

question: What's the difference between devised theatre and performing a scripted play, and which do you prefer working on?
lookingFor: A clear understanding of devising as a collaboratively generated process versus interpreting an existing text, with a genuine preference backed by reasoning.

bullets: Explain devising as building original material collaboratively, often from improvisation or research
Contrast it with the interpretive work of scripted performance
State a genuine preference with reasoning, not just whichever sounds more impressive
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: With a script you're interpreting someone else's words, finding your own truth within a fixed structure, whereas devising means the group is generating the material itself, often starting from an image, a piece of research, or an improvisation and shaping it into a structure as you go. I actually prefer devising, even though it's messier and more frightening because there's no safety net of an existing text, because I like that everyone's voice genuinely shapes the piece rather than just the writer's. That said, working on scripts has taught me discipline that I bring back into devising, like being precise about what a moment is actually doing.

commonMistakes: Describing devising as simply improvising with no structure
Claiming a preference with no reasoning behind it
Treating scripted work as inherently less creative
followUps: What's the hardest part of devising as a group?

question: Who is your favourite playwright, and why?
lookingFor: Genuine engagement with a specific playwright's work, with reasoning that goes beyond reputation.

bullets: Name a specific playwright and at least one specific play by them
Explain what specifically about their style or concerns resonates
Avoid choosing purely because the name sounds impressive
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I keep coming back to Caryl Churchill, particularly Top Girls, because of how fearlessly she breaks conventional structure, that opening dinner party scene with women from across history all talking over each other still amazes me every time I reread it. She trusts the audience to work for meaning instead of handing it to them, and that ambition is what I want from theatre. I also admire that her plays are never just formally clever, they're always in service of a real political question underneath.

commonMistakes: Naming a famous playwright with no specific play or reason
Choosing someone purely because they think it sounds impressive to the panel
Confusing the playwright's biography with their actual work
followUps: Is there anything about their work you find weaker or less convincing?

question: Why do you think Shakespeare's plays are still performed so widely today?
lookingFor: A thoughtful answer that goes beyond 'he's a genius' toward specific reasons like universal themes, flexible staging, or language.

bullets: Identify at least one specific reason, such as universal human themes or open staging directions
Give a concrete example from a play or production
Avoid a purely reputation-based answer
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Part of it is that the plays deal with things that never stop being relevant, ambition, jealousy, grief, and they do it with characters complicated enough to reinterpret endlessly. But I also think it's practical, the scripts have almost no fixed staging directions, so a director can set Macbeth in a corporate boardroom or a war zone and the text still holds. I saw a modern-dress Julius Caesar set during a contemporary election campaign and it felt disturbingly current, which shows how open the plays really are to reinvention.

commonMistakes: A vague 'he's the greatest writer ever' answer with no substance
Treating the plays as museum pieces rather than living texts
No concrete example from a specific play or production
followUps: Is there a Shakespeare play you think doesn't hold up as well? Why?

question: What can physical theatre communicate that dialogue-heavy plays can't?
lookingFor: Understanding that movement, gesture, and the body can carry meaning text cannot, with a specific example.

bullets: Identify what physical theatre foregrounds that text-based theatre doesn't, such as pre-verbal emotion or rhythm
Name a company, practitioner, or production as an example
Avoid suggesting physical theatre is simply 'acting without words'
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Physical theatre can get at something before language, the instinctive, animal parts of a feeling that words sometimes flatten out. I saw a Frantic Assembly piece where a whole argument between a couple was expressed through a movement sequence, bodies pulling toward and away from each other, and it communicated the relationship's power imbalance more precisely than dialogue might have, because there was nowhere for the actors to hide behind clever lines. It made me think about how much meaning gets carried in rhythm, weight, and proximity that a script alone can't show.

commonMistakes: Describing physical theatre as just mime or acting without talking
No specific practitioner or production named as an example
Suggesting physical theatre is less sophisticated than text-based work
followUps: Have you performed any physical theatre yourself? What was that like?

question: What do you think a director actually does, beyond telling actors where to stand?
lookingFor: A grounded understanding of directing as interpretive and collaborative leadership, not just traffic control.

bullets: Describe the director's interpretive role, shaping a single vision of the text
Mention collaboration with actors and designers, not just top-down control
Give a specific example from directing experience or observation
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A director's real job is building a single coherent interpretation out of a text that could support many, and then getting an entire team, actors, designers, everyone, pulling toward that same vision without flattening anyone's individual contribution. When I directed a short piece last year, most of my time wasn't blocking, it was asking actors questions in rehearsal to help them find choices that served the interpretation I had in mind, rather than just dictating moves to them. The best directors I've watched work seem to lead by asking good questions as much as by giving instructions.

commonMistakes: Reducing directing to blocking and stage traffic
Describing directing as purely dictatorial with no collaboration
No personal example or observation to back up the answer
followUps: Have you directed anything yourself? What was the hardest part?

subtopic: Handling a difficult scene as an actor
question: Tell us about a role or scene you found genuinely difficult to get right. How did you work through it?
lookingFor: Honest reflection on a real creative struggle and a concrete process for solving it, not a story where everything went smoothly.

bullets: Name a specific role or scene and what exactly made it hard
Describe concrete steps taken, such as research, rehearsal choices, or feedback
Show what actually changed in the performance as a result
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I played a grieving mother in a scene where I kept playing the sadness too big and generic, and my director kept telling me it read as performed rather than felt. I went away and wrote a full backstory for the character, including the exact moment she found out, and in the next rehearsal I tried playing the scene almost flat, trying to hold the grief in rather than display it. That restraint ended up being far more affecting than my original choice, and it taught me that specificity beats intensity almost every time.

commonMistakes: Choosing a story with no real struggle in it
Vague description of 'working hard' with no specific technique used
No clear change in the outcome
followUps: What feedback from a director has changed how you act since?

question: Is it harder to write, direct, or perform tragedy or comedy? What's your view?
lookingFor: A genuine, reasoned opinion showing understanding of the demands of both forms, not a shallow cliche about comedy being harder.

bullets: Take a clear position rather than refusing to choose
Give a specific reason grounded in craft, such as timing, tone, or audience trust
Acknowledge the other form's difficulty too, showing balanced thinking
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I actually think comedy is harder to perform, because the timing has to be exact, a beat too slow or fast and the laugh just doesn't land, and there's nowhere to hide because you get instant feedback from the audience's silence. Tragedy has more room to breathe, an audience will forgive an imperfect pace if the emotion is honest. That said, writing tragedy well without tipping into melodrama is its own enormous skill, so I don't think either is simply easier, they just demand different kinds of precision.

commonMistakes: Refusing to take any position
Repeating the cliche 'comedy is harder' with no actual reasoning
Dismissing the other genre as simply easy
followUps: Which do you personally prefer performing?

question: Describe a production where the set or design choices really shaped how you understood the play.
lookingFor: The ability to analyse design as an active storytelling element, not just decoration.

bullets: Name a specific production and describe the design choice concretely
Explain how it changed meaning or emphasis, not just how it looked
Connect the design choice back to the text or themes
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I saw a production of A Doll's House staged in a rotating glass box, so the audience could see the whole apartment at once, including rooms the characters thought were private. It completely changed how I read the play, turning the audience into witnesses to a kind of surveillance the characters didn't know they were under, which mirrored Nora's own hidden life catching up with her. It made me realise design isn't just setting, it can actually argue a specific interpretation of the text.

commonMistakes: Describing a set purely in terms of how attractive it looked
No connection made between the design and the play's meaning
Vague memory with no specific production named
followUps: If you were designing that production, what would you have done differently?

question: How do you respond when a director or teacher gives you notes you disagree with?
lookingFor: Maturity around receiving feedback, distinguishing between defensive resistance and thoughtful pushback.

bullets: Show a default of trying the note before rejecting it
Describe a specific, appropriate way of raising genuine disagreement
Avoid sounding either doormat-like or dismissive of direction
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My instinct is to try the note in the room first, because sometimes what feels wrong to me as the actor reads completely differently from outside, and directors usually have a reason even when they don't spell it out. But if I've tried it and I genuinely think it's damaging the character, I'll ask rather than argue, something like 'can you help me understand what you're going for here', which usually either clarifies the note or opens a real conversation about it. I try not to be someone who just complies silently either, because a director loses something if actors never push back at all.

commonMistakes: Claiming to always agree with every note with no critical thinking
Sounding like they'd argue with directors regularly
No concrete strategy, just a general claim of being 'open to feedback'
followUps: Tell us about a time a note actually changed your mind about a choice.

question: Does theatre have a responsibility to address social or political issues, or is that not its job?
lookingFor: A reasoned, non-dogmatic position that engages with genuine tension in the question rather than a flat yes or no.

bullets: Acknowledge the range of theatre's purposes, from pure entertainment to activism
Take a considered position with a specific example
Avoid implying all theatre must be political to matter
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I don't think every play has to carry a political message, some of the best theatre I've seen was just interested in being beautifully made, and that has value too. But I do think theatre has a unique capacity for putting an audience physically in the same room as an issue, which is different from reading about it, and plays like Sweat used that to make economic decline feel human rather than statistical in a way that stayed with me. So I'd say theatre isn't obligated to be political, but when it chooses to be, it can do things other media can't.

commonMistakes: A flat 'yes, all theatre must be political' or 'no, theatre is just entertainment' with no nuance
No specific example to ground the argument
Avoiding taking any real position at all
followUps: Can a play be both entertaining and politically serious? Give an example.

question: Is a play really finished when it's written, or only when it's performed?
lookingFor: Engagement with the tension between drama as literature and as a live event, showing awareness this is a genuine debate.

bullets: Recognise both positions as defensible rather than dismissing one outright
Explain what performance specifically adds that reading a script cannot
Reach a considered personal view rather than sitting entirely on the fence
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: You can absolutely study a script as literature, close-reading imagery and structure the way you would a poem, and that has real value. But I think a play is written to be completed in performance, because so much of what a script implies, silences, tempo, the specific way a line lands differently on different nights, only exists once actors and an audience are in the room together. I've read plays that felt flat on the page and came alive completely differently in production, which convinces me the script is really more like a blueprint than the finished building.

commonMistakes: Dismissing the value of reading plays as literature entirely
Refusing to actually commit to a position
Treating the question as if there's an obviously correct textbook answer
followUps: Can you think of a play that reads very differently from how it performs?

question: What do you know about the role of the chorus in Ancient Greek theatre, and why has it largely disappeared from modern plays?
lookingFor: Basic factual grounding in theatre history plus some thoughtful reasoning about why theatrical conventions change over time.

bullets: Correctly describe the chorus's function, commenting on action, voicing communal perspective, or linking scenes
Note it was tied to specific religious and civic contexts in Ancient Greece
Offer a reasonable explanation for its decline, such as the rise of psychological realism and the individual protagonist
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The chorus in Greek theatre acted almost like the voice of the community, commenting on the action, reacting to events, sometimes warning characters, and it grew out of religious festivals where group song and dance were central. As theatre moved toward naturalism and a focus on individual psychology, especially from the nineteenth century onward, there was less room for a group commenting from outside the action, since the form prioritised private, internal experience instead. That said, I think the chorus never fully vanished, it just changed shape, you see traces of it in things like ensemble narration in more presentational contemporary work.

commonMistakes: No understanding of the chorus's actual function beyond 'a group that sings'
Treating the chorus as unique to musicals with no historical grounding
No attempt to explain why the convention changed
followUps: Can you name a modern play or production that revives a chorus-like device?

question: How comfortable are you with improvisation, and what's a time it went badly or well?
lookingFor: Honest self-assessment of a real skill area, with a specific memory rather than a generic claim of confidence.

bullets: Give an honest, specific self-assessment rather than a blanket claim
Describe one concrete improvisation experience, good or bad
Reflect on what it revealed about their strengths or areas to develop
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'm reasonably confident with improvisation now, but it wasn't always that way, I remember completely freezing during a first-year improv exercise because I was so focused on being funny that I forgot to actually listen to my scene partner. What changed things was a workshop that drilled the idea of accepting offers rather than blocking them, saying yes to whatever your partner gives you and building on it. Since then improvisation has become one of my favourite parts of rehearsal, because it forces me to stay genuinely present instead of relying on planned choices.

commonMistakes: Claiming total confidence with no specific example to back it up
Describing improvisation purely as being funny or quick-witted
No honest reflection on a struggle or growth area
followUps: What makes a good scene partner in an improvised scene?

question: What would you bring to our department's productions and rehearsal rooms beyond your own performances?
lookingFor: Awareness that a theatre course is a collaborative ensemble, with specific, credible contributions beyond just acting talent.

bullets: Name specific skills or attitudes, not just enthusiasm
Show awareness that a course thrives on more than performers alone
Ground the claim in past evidence of actually contributing that way
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd bring a genuine willingness to work backstage as much as on stage, which I don't think everyone auditioning would say honestly, but running sound for two productions taught me how much I enjoy problem-solving under pressure during a live show. I also tend to be the person in rehearsal who asks the awkward clarifying question when a scene isn't landing, which has occasionally unstuck a whole rehearsal. I'd want to bring that same mix of hands-on flexibility and honest feedback into your productions.

commonMistakes: Only talking about their own performance ambitions
Vague claims of being 'a team player' with no evidence
Overselling skills they haven't actually demonstrated
followUps: Tell us about a time you supported someone else's work rather than your own.

subtopic: Adapting a text to a new context
question: If you could set any existing play in a completely different time or place, which would you choose and why would it work?
lookingFor: Creative, well-reasoned directorial thinking, showing the applicant can justify an interpretive choice rather than just picking something novel.

bullets: Name a specific play and a specific new setting
Explain concretely what the new context would illuminate in the text
Acknowledge at least one risk or challenge the choice creates
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd set An Enemy of the People in the middle of a modern social media pandemic, misinformation storm, because the play is really about a lone truth-teller against a town that would rather protect its economy than face facts, and that tension feels almost exactly like current arguments over public health and online outrage. Doing it with characters live-tweeting and town meetings turning into viral pile-ons would make the mob dynamics feel immediate rather than historical. The risk is it could tip into being too on-the-nose or dated within a few years, so I'd want the design to stay slightly abstract rather than literally recreating a specific platform.

commonMistakes: Choosing a setting purely for shock value with no real justification
No acknowledgment of any risk or downside to the choice
Vague reasoning that doesn't connect the new setting to the play's actual themes
followUps: What would be lost by moving it out of its original setting?

question: How do you deal with nerves before going on stage?
lookingFor: Honest acknowledgment that nerves are normal, with a concrete personal strategy rather than a claim of never being nervous.

bullets: Acknowledge nerves honestly rather than claiming immunity to them
Describe a specific, personal coping strategy
Show understanding that some nervous energy can actually help a performance
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I still get properly nervous before every opening night, and I've stopped trying to make that go away because I've realised the nerves usually mean I care about getting it right. What helps is a very specific warm-up routine, physical stretches and running my first three lines out loud backstage, because it gives my nervous energy somewhere concrete to go instead of just spinning. I've learned the goal isn't calm, it's channeling the adrenaline into focus rather than panic.

commonMistakes: Claiming to never feel nervous at all
No specific coping technique, just a vague 'I try to relax'
Treating nerves as purely a problem rather than potentially useful energy
followUps: Has a performance ever gone wrong because of nerves? What happened?

question: What do you think is the biggest barrier to making theatre more accessible or representative, and what could change it?
lookingFor: Genuine industry awareness of real barriers, such as ticket cost, training access, or casting practices, with a considered, non-superficial suggestion.

bullets: Name a specific, real barrier rather than a vague statement about 'inclusion'
Show awareness of why the barrier exists, not just that it does
Suggest a concrete, plausible change rather than a slogan
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think cost is one of the biggest and most underdiscussed barriers, both ticket prices that shut people out of watching theatre and the unpaid or low-paid entry routes into training and early career work that shut out people who can't afford to work for free. I saw this firsthand volunteering with a youth theatre where kids who were genuinely talented dropped out once fees for the next level of training came up. I think schemes offering paid entry-level placements and pay-what-you-can nights matter more than most representation initiatives that focus only on casting, because they address who gets to be in the room in the first place.

commonMistakes: A vague statement about diversity with no specific barrier named
No understanding of why the barrier actually exists
A slogan-like answer with no concrete suggestion for change
followUps: Have you seen or been part of any initiative that actually addressed this?

question: What kind of work do you hope to be doing in theatre five or ten years after this course, and how will studying help you get there?
lookingFor: A grounded, realistic sense of direction within theatre that connects specifically to what the course offers, while allowing for flexibility.

bullets: Give a direction within theatre, whether performing, directing, writing, or another path
Show realistic awareness that the industry is unpredictable and paths shift
Connect the ambition specifically to skills or experiences the course provides
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd like to end up writing and directing my own new work, ideally through a small company rather than chasing a single big break, because the pieces I've cared most about making have always come from projects I helped shape from the ground up. I know that path is unstable and I might end up doing a mix of teaching, freelance directing, and my own projects to make it sustainable, and I'm fine with that. This course's dramaturgy and directing modules, plus the chance to devise original work every year, are exactly the training ground I think that career needs.

commonMistakes: An unrealistically specific plan, like naming one exact theatre company as the only acceptable outcome
No connection between the ambition and what the course actually offers
Sounding like they'll abandon theatre entirely if the first opportunity doesn't work out
followUps: What would you do if that specific path didn't work out?
